newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Margins worry refiners.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Margins worry refiners.

text.p: Asian crude prices are expected to come under renewed pressure this week with the prospects of refinery run cuts amid squeezed margins playing on traders minds.
They said the run up in global crude and cash prices was putting renewed pressure on refinery margins in Singapore as product prices ease.
"Margins are tight. If it carries on like this you are looking at run cuts," one trader at an oil major said on Monday.
"Premiums have to come off," he said.
Refinery margins were strong in the first quarter of the year as crude prices fell and as gas oil was supported by massive buying by a group of traders, including Hin Leong Trading in Singapore.
But the gas oil buying has waned, taking away the support for product prices, just as crude prices have been ignited by a technical rally.
On Friday London's July Brent contract rose 86 cents per barrel to $20.35 and June NYMEX crude rose 82 cents in New York to $22.12.
Tightening availabilities of North Sea crude added to the futures' rally.
Margins are now negative, or verging on the negative so refineries are taking a close look at the prospects for June regional and July Middle East trading, traders said.
Traders in Asia said the tightening margins could be exacerbated by the return of refineries from turnaround -- adding product supply and supporting the crude through buying.

In addition, some June loading Middle East crudes are still trying to find a home. One oil major was heard looking to sell as much as 1.5 million barrels of June Oman, when most refineries in Asia were already shifting to consider their July-lifting programme.
Traders said light grades could find the greatest downward pressure among crude oils, simply because seasonally many refineries have moved over to the medium type grades.
But even Minas or Duri could be undermined by the worries over refinery margins.
The Minas premium doubled late last week to ICP +30 cents amid speculation that the export allocation for June would be as low as 20-30,000 barrels.
In fact, the allocation was 62,000 barrels per day (bpd), down from 73,000 in May and lead some traders to expect an easing in the premium.
The overall allocation was around 175-180,000 barrels per day.
However, the Duri allocation was cut back to 33,000 bpd from 60,000 in June. Cinta was cut to 4,000 bpd from 14,000 and Bontang Mix to 18,000 bpd from 35,000.
Traders said the main cause for the lower allocations was a new 60,000 bpd crude unit coming up at the Balikpapan refinery in Indonesia during June or early July.
Pertamina is expected to test feed Minas, Arun, Cinta, Widuri and Duri during the month, reducing export availabilities.
But traders said the price support from reduced availabilities might be partly offset by worries over margins.

Refineries might be relucant to buy into a rising market premium if margins are too tight, especially if the arbitrage for West African imports is still open -- as indicated by a July Brent/Dubai of $0.95/$1.05 per barrel.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
